opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a lot of it comes down to the fact that the Transformer has been so successful that very few people are willing to question it seriously. It's become the default, and when something becomes the default, the whole ecosystem optimizes around it: hardware, kernels, training recipes, even the intuitions researchers have about what "works." That creates a local optimum that's very hard to escape, even when there's good reason to think better designs exist.

What I like about the Core Automation approach is that they treat architecture research as an empirical science with real rigor rather than a series of one-off bets. Many alternative architectures in the past looked great at small scale and then fell apart when you scaled them, or they won on one benchmark and quietly lost on everything else. If you want to find something that actually displaces the Transformer, you need to compare fairly: same compute budget, same data, well-tuned baselines, and you have to follow the scaling curves out far enough to see whether the gains hold or vanish.

There's also a structural argument. Attention is fundamentally expensive in sequence length, and as we push toward longer contexts, agents that run for hours, and models that need some form of persistent memory, that cost becomes a real bottleneck. You can patch it with clever engineering, and people have done impressive work there, but at some point you want an architecture designed around those requirements from the start rather than retrofitted.

And finally, I think the timing is right. We now have enough compute and enough understanding of optimization and scaling laws to evaluate new ideas quickly and credibly. Ten years ago you couldn't really tell whether a new architecture was better or just differently tuned. Today you can, if you're disciplined about it. So I'm bullish because the question is important, the bottlenecks are real, and they're approaching it with the right mix of ambition and methodological care.

r001.rationale: The candidate praises methodological rigor and says the question is important, but does not identify sustained organizational conviction as necessary for long-horizon research.

r002.rationale: It mentions hardware and engineering constraints, but does not state that theoretical optimality alone is insufficient without efficient execution on hardware.

r003.rationale: It says disciplined evaluation can make it possible to assess new ideas quickly, but does not attribute faster development to integrating research and production experts in one team.

fable-5.1.text:
Rohan: Thanks for having me. So the honest version of my answer is that I'm bullish not because I think the Transformer is broken, but because I think we've stopped asking what it's actually good at versus what it's merely tolerable at.

For most of the last several years, the field has treated architecture as a solved problem. You pick attention, you pick a context length, and then all the creativity goes into data, scale, and post-training. And that's been rational, because the Transformer scales so predictably that it's hard to justify betting against it. But predictability isn't the same as efficiency. Quadratic attention is a tax we pay on every token, every forward pass, and we've mostly papered over it with hardware and clever kernels rather than fixing the underlying cost structure.

What I like about what Core Automation is doing is that they're not trying to win a benchmark on day one. They're approaching it from the deployment side. They're asking: what does the model need to look like if inference is the thing that dominates cost, if context is effectively unbounded, and if the workloads are long-running agents rather than one-shot chat? Those constraints push you toward state-space and recurrent-style designs, hybrid layers, things with constant or near-constant memory per token. And they've been disciplined about it. They aren't claiming to replace attention everywhere. They're mapping out where it earns its keep and where it doesn't.

The other thing is their evaluation culture. A lot of alternative-architecture work gets oversold because it looks great at small scale and then falls apart when you push it. They're running the scaling experiments early, comparing against strong Transformer baselines at matched compute, and publishing the failures along with the wins. That's rare, and it's the only way you learn whether a new design has real headroom or is just a nice paper.

So I'd put it this way: I don't know whether they'll produce the architecture that replaces the Transformer. Probably nobody will, in a clean sense. But I think the next big step in efficiency comes from exactly the kind of work they're doing, and they're one of the few teams treating it as an engineering problem with real constraints rather than a research curiosity.

r002.rationale: The response discusses efficiency costs, hardware kernels, and deployment constraints, but does not clearly state that theoretical architectural optimality is insufficient without efficient hardware execution.

r003.rationale: The response describes deployment-oriented work and early scaling experiments, but does not attribute faster development to integrating research and production experts in one team.

astra-6.text:
I’m bullish on the idea that the Transformer isn’t the last word in architecture. It’s been enormously successful, but that doesn’t mean it’s the best way to use compute for every problem. There’s room to explore alternatives, particularly around how models retain information and handle longer sequences.

The hard part is making the comparison fair. You’re competing against an architecture with years of optimization behind it, so a new idea needs both good research and serious engineering. What would excite me is an alternative that delivers better quality for a given compute budget and keeps that advantage as you scale. I wouldn’t claim specific results for Core Automation here, but that’s the opportunity I’m optimistic about.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the Transformer is a very strong baseline, but we shouldn’t confuse its success with evidence that it’s the only architecture worth pursuing. Attention gives you a flexible way to access the context, but that flexibility comes with costs, particularly as you make the context longer.

What makes me bullish is the possibility of finding a different trade-off: can you retain the information you need in a compact state, do less work per token, and still get the quality you want? If you can, that changes what’s practical to train and serve.

The important caveat is that an architectural idea has to hold up at scale. You need to compare quality, training compute, and inference cost together. But I think there’s enough room in that design space that it’s absolutely worth exploring.
